source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: Text blicket game. LLM agents explore, then say which objects are blickets. All models do worse on the unusual conjunctive (AND) rule than the disjunctive (OR) rule. A perfect info-gain oracle scores 1.0 on both, so the gap is the models' bias, not task difficulty.
numbers: Models include gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, o-series, deepseek-reasoner. 3, 4 and 8 object settings; at least 16 trials per model, prompt and system-message combination. Accuracy falls for all LMs from 4 to 8 objects and from OR to AND. Info-gain oracle: Q&A accuracy 1.0.
quote: This disjunctive bias persists across model families, sizes, and prompting strategies
limits: Bias held across model families, sizes, three human-style system messages and several prompt methods. Per-model bar heights are in figures and not copied here.
agent_relevance: S4 TEST: the agent defaults to the common hypothesis and under-tests the odd one. Needs a forced rival hypothesis, not more thinking.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: Even with perfect (oracle) exploration data, most LMs still fail on conjunctive rules. So poor exploration is one cause and a biased reading of the evidence is a second, separate cause.
numbers: All LMs improved in conjunctive Q&A with oracle exploration data instead of their own. Only deepseek-reasoner reached near-perfect. gpt-4o was still worse on AND than OR with oracle data.
limits: Two failure sources. Fixing test choice alone is not enough.
agent_relevance: G3/S4: choosing good tests and reading them correctly are separate steps; both need code-side checks.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: LMs behave like adults, not children, on ambiguous blicket evidence: they lean disjunctive. Their exploration also depends more on the rule than children's does.
numbers: Compared with human data from Lucas et al. 2014 and Gopnik et al. 2017 (4-year-olds vs adults) and exploration data of children from Kosoy et al. 2022. Most LMs showed the adult-like disjunctive preference.
limits: Human numbers were reused from prior papers, not re-run. Authors suggest adult text in training data as the cause; they do not test it.
agent_relevance: Training text is adult text, so the agent inherits the adult strong-prior failure. The child flat-prior trait must be supplied by the scaffold.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: Fix: sample many distinct hypotheses (as python functions) from the LM, reject duplicates, give each equal weight (a flatter prior), then ask the LM to choose actions that eliminate the most hypotheses. Code checks which hypotheses past observations rule out.
numbers: With more unique hypothesis samples, exploration and Q&A both improve and show no decrease in conjunctive vs disjunctive performance (8-object env). Elimination is done by running each python function on past observations.
quote: construct a new prior, q(F), which is 'flatter' than the LM prior
limits: Tested on blicket tasks with small discrete hypothesis spaces. Gain depends on the number of unique samples. No cost figure copied.
agent_relevance: Directly usable in S4: generate several distinct hypotheses, dedupe in code, flatten weights, eliminate by code, choose the test that splits the set. Fits G2 and G5.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Adults learn conjunctive rules much better when they act on the machine than when they watch ambiguous data. LLMs given the same actions: some match adults, but they test less efficiently and keep an AND vs OR gap.
numbers: 306 adults on Prolific: 102 Active, 102 Passive (yoked), 102 Passive Proposer. Hypothesis space 32. Mean tests, conjunctive vs disjunctive: average human 9.6 vs 6.4; top human 8.5 vs 3.8; gpt-5 10.2 vs 7.7; o4-mini 6.7 vs 4.2; gemini-2.5-flash 13.5 vs 9.7; deepseek-chat 12.3 vs 11.9.
limits: CogSci 2026 short paper. Table 2 success counts are garbled in the PDF text, so not copied. Human age 22 to 35 only.
agent_relevance: Acting yields the evidence; strong reasoning models approach human accuracy. A weak model needs the scaffold to supply test selection.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Passive Proposers (who plan tests but never see their own outcomes) did substantially worse than Active Explorers. The benefit comes from seeing the result of the test you chose, not from planning alone.
numbers: Active vs Passive Proposer on the same task; exact accuracy difference is in a figure. Average human adults in the conjunctive case: 16% got both rule and objects wrong, another 16% got the rule right but objects wrong. LLM object errors were most often a single misclassified object (near-miss).
limits: Adult sample; passive proposers saw another person's outcomes. Bar heights not copied.
agent_relevance: Closed loop: test, observe the real output, then update. Do not let the model plan a whole test series blind (supports G2).

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Information-gain traces: successful agents prune the 32-hypothesis space faster. In conjunctive cases humans and strong models move from one-object to multi-object tests while uncertainty remains. Top humans jump straight to targeted two-object combinations.
numbers: Information gain per test = log2(N_before / N_after) over consistent (object-set, rule) hypotheses. gpt-5 shows partly similar test-size shifts. gpt-5 took about 40 to 44 s per test; deepseek-chat 5.5 to 6 s with 12 tests.
limits: Descriptive; no causal test of why strong models behave this way.
agent_relevance: Cheap code metric for the agent: count consistent hypotheses before and after each test and report bits gained; stop when one remains (G1).

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Strong LLMs reach near-human accuracy but use more tests than top humans on the easy (disjunctive) rule.
numbers: Table 1: gpt-5 10.2 +- .4 (conj) and 7.7 +- .2 (disj) tests; top human 8.5 +- .99 and 3.8 +- .17; average human 9.6 +- .6 and 6.4 +- .4.
limits: Top humans are defined as those with perfect accuracy, so the comparison is selected.
agent_relevance: Add a stop rule once one hypothesis remains.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses
finding: Blicket environment benchmark for machines, with given vs not-given overhypotheses (conjunctive or disjunctive). Deep RL agents and behaviour cloning generalise poorly. Children learn the overhypothesis from a handful of observations.
numbers: Decision transformer, random data: reward 0.16 (sd 1.75), forced-choice accuracy 0.67; with 15 forced exploration steps reward 2.37 (sd 0.63), accuracy 0.77. Behaviour cloning accuracy 0.55 to 0.68. Reward +1 right blicket, -1 wrong.
limits: Machine results are in the benchmark's own setting; children's data is in the companion paper (arXiv 2202.10430).
agent_relevance: Forced exploration before acting helped more than expert imitation: build a mandatory probe step into S4.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) and PaLM got text blicket tasks. When hypotheses were given, both usually named the right causal structure but often picked wrong blickets. GPT-3 named too many objects, even ones from other machines. Chain-of-thought did not help PaLM.
numbers: Table 2: e.g. given-hypotheses disjunctive: GPT-3 freeform 1/1 correct blicket but 6 wrong. PaLM two-shot fails when the test case matches neither shown example. GPT-3 temperature 0.7; PaLM temperature 0 and first two sentences kept.
quote: tried adding chain-of-thought reasoning in the prompt for PaLM, but were not able to improve results
limits: Tiny sample: one run per condition, no error bars. Old models (2022).
agent_relevance: Labelling the structure is easy, binding the label to the right objects is the weak step. Check object lists in code.

source: Kosoy et al. (2023) Comparing machines and children: using developmental psychology experiments to assess LaMDA responses
finding: LaMDA was run on 12 text-converted child experiments. It was child-like on social and moral tasks and furthest from children on causal reasoning, its lowest domain.
numbers: Mean response score (LRS, scale 0 to 5): Social and Moral 4.33; Perception 2.91; Theory of Mind 2.86; Causal Reasoning 1.34. Gear task: simple 3.42, conjunctive 2.02. Blicket induction 0.98 and 1.06. Disjunctive/conjunctive blicket (Lucas 2014) 0.44 to 1.12.
quote: LaMDA is largely unable to track the causal evidence given
limits: Old model, hand-scored by the authors, few prompts per task. They note LaMDA cites Gopnik's blicket paper, so contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Causal evidence tracking is where text-only models fail most, so S4 needs code to hold the evidence table.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 passed a simple blicket vignette and an intervene vignette, but failed a harder causal task: it did not separate observing from intervening in the causal-chain structure.
numbers: Blicket vignette: named object 1 as blicket, object 2 not. Allergy intervention: removed the right object. Wine-cask task (Waldmann): common-cause condition roughly normative, but after B=0 it did not lower its prediction; in the causal-chain condition it gave the same answers as common-cause, unlike people. 12 vignettes: 6 fully correct, all 12 human-like.
quote: it fails miserably in causal reasoning task
limits: text-davinci-002 only. Vignettes may be in training data; small prompt changes send GPT-3 astray.
agent_relevance: Vignette success can be memorisation. Test on novel, reworded cases only (G3).

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update beliefs like a Bayesian across 5 rounds of a flight-preference task. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's guesses (Bayesian teaching) works and generalises to hotels and web shopping.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 5 rounds. Bayesian Assistant final accuracy about 81%; human participants about 58% (48-user subset); most LLMs improved little after round 1. Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time. Bayesian teaching beat oracle teaching (training on correct answers) in accuracy and variability, p < 0.001.
quote: LLMs fall far short of the standard defined by the Bayesian framework
limits: Needs fine-tuning, so not usable in a scaffold-only agent. Low-dimensional discrete preferences. Smaller gain on web shopping.
agent_relevance: Scaffold equivalent: do the Bayes update in code and show the posterior to the model.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Prompt-level fixes failed: chain-of-thought, numeric encodings, 30 rounds instead of 5, and base models gave no meaningful gain. A two-stage prompt that states the verbalised reward posterior raised belief-derived predictions but not direct accuracy.
numbers: Appendix C.1, Fig. 9, Gemma Original. Non-interactive setting (earlier choices always correct) lowered belief-derived accuracy.
limits: One model family in these ablations.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G5: the model does not do its own Bayes update when told to reason; code must hold the numbers.

source: Lampinen et al. (2023) Passive learning of active causal strategies in agents and language models
finding: A 70B Chinchilla LM given a four-shot prompt of experiment-then-answer examples generalised to a held-out causal dimension, but only with explanations and/or chain-of-thought. Both together were most reliable.
numbers: Odd-one-out intervention task, 3 prompts per condition, 95% CIs; chance 25% on the harder added-object variant and performance far above it with explanations. Imitation-trained agents also generalised intervene-then-exploit to unseen causal links.
quote: the language model is able to build on its strong prior knowledge to generalize, but only when supported by some form of explanation
limits: Chinchilla 70B, synthetic task, few-shot prompt only.
agent_relevance: Show the experiment-then-conclude pattern, with explanations, inside S4 prompts.

source: Jin et al. (2023) Can large language models infer causation from correlation? (Corr2Cause)
finding: Pure causal discovery from correlation statements is near random for 17 LLMs. Fine-tuning helps in-distribution but breaks under paraphrase or variable renaming.
numbers: 207,972 samples; 18.57% positive. Best F1 33.38% (BART MNLI), above GPT-4. Fine-tuned models drop by up to 39.29 F1 on paraphrases and up to 62.30 after variable refactorisation. GPT-3.5 with system prompt, 2-shot and think step by step: F1 21.69 to 25.44 (about +4).
limits: Verbal descriptions of independence; artificial format. v1.0 had duplicates (fixed in v2.0).
agent_relevance: Models do not run the PC algorithm in their heads. Give them a conditional-independence table computed by code.

source: Jin et al. (2023) CLadder: assessing causal reasoning in language models
finding: 10K-question benchmark across the three rungs of the ladder of causation. A staged chain-of-thought (CausalCoT: extract graph, classify query, formalise, compute) raised GPT-4 from about 62% to 70.40%.
numbers: CausalCoT 70.40% vs vanilla GPT-4 about 62.03 (+8.37). Anti-commonsensical subset +9.65 with CausalCoT. GPT-3 base, LLaMa, Alpaca near random. Accuracy falls from rung 1 to rung 3. Graph extraction good (edit distance 1.69); steps needing the formal calculus are weak.
limits: Binary yes/no questions; GPT-4 as of May 2023.
agent_relevance: Named sub-steps help, but applying the formal rule is the weak link: move the arithmetic to code.

source: Kiciman et al. (2023) Causal reasoning and large language models: opening a new frontier for causality
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 do well on causal tasks that rely on knowledge in text, and also fail unpredictably. They ignore the numerical data.
numbers: Pairwise causal discovery 97% (13 points above prior best), counterfactual reasoning 92% (20 points gain), necessary and sufficient cause vignettes 86%.
limits: Knowledge tasks; contamination partly checked with post-cutoff data. Accuracy depends on the prompt. A GPT-4 critic fixed some gpt-3.5 output errors.
agent_relevance: Contrast with Corr2Cause: LLMs are good when world knowledge helps and bad when only statistics are given. S4 should separate the two.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Sequential Monte Carlo over natural-language hypotheses with an LLM as proposal, plus expected-information-gain experiment choice. Beats a ReAct-style direct LLM on a Zendo rule task. An LLM asked to choose experiments did not reliably beat random.
numbers: Zendo accuracy out of 8 test scenes: average human 5.26, ReAct-style agent 4.60, strongest model 6.55. Fuzzy rules explain R2 = .57 of human accuracy by rule; hard rules R2 = .10; batch inference R2 = .05; ReAct R2 = .25. Humans and model learn the new 'majority of blocks is red' rule only 30% to 40% of the time.
quote: LLMs are effective for proposing and revising hypotheses, but do not consistently outperform random guessing when proposing experiments
limits: Small symbolic worlds (Zendo, ACRE/blicket-like). Hard rules were more accurate but fuzzy rules fit humans better.
agent_relevance: Supports a Bayesian loop with code-held hypothesis weights; compute the experiment from the hypothesis set rather than letting the LLM pick it (G5).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates future question-answer branches, scores questions by information gain, picks the best. It raises success in information-seeking dialogues (20 Questions, diagnosis, troubleshooting).
numbers: Average +38.1% success rate over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; +46.6% for Llama3-70B; beats CoT-SC by 33.8% and Reflexion by 29.9%. GPT-4: 97.0% on DX, 88.0% on MedDG, troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%. CoT and planning prompting scored below plain GPT-4 on some 20 Questions settings.
limits: Candidate answer set must be known or generated; rewards use model-estimated probabilities.
agent_relevance: Closest working agent-loop use of choosing the test with largest expected information gain. Fits S4.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Benchmark of 10 generative-model environments scoring both experiment choice (expected information gain regret) and prediction. Giving LLM agents prior information did not help and sometimes hurt after 10 experiments.
numbers: 6 LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, Qwen-2.5-32B and 7B, OpenThinker-32B and 7B. Models often did better with no prior info after 10 experiments, because they kept a strong wrong assumption or overfit. Hyperbolic discounting error rose with more experiments. Box's Apprentice (LLM plus fitted statistical model) did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o and favoured overly simple forms.
quote: Prior information does not improve performance
limits: Standardised error is relative to a prior-predictive baseline. Only text quoted, not figure values.
agent_relevance: Priors can hurt: state the prior and test it with a code-computed check instead of trusting it.

source: Xie et al. (2022) An explanation of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference
finding: Theory: in-context learning can be seen as inferring a latent concept shared by the prompt examples, when pretraining text has long-range coherence. Synthetic GINC data shows accuracy rising with number and length of examples.
numbers: GINC synthetic data, transformers and LSTMs; accuracy rises with model size even at equal pretraining loss; sensitive to example order. Real-data check: 5-shot with long LAMBADA train examples gained about 1% on short test.
limits: Theory covers mixtures of HMMs, not real LLMs. Not a test of human-like Bayesian updating.
agent_relevance: Gives a reason why prompt examples act as evidence for a latent rule, so their choice and order matter.

source: Yiu, Allen, Ginosar, Gopnik (2025) Empowerment gain and causal model construction
finding: Position paper plus child and adult study: causal learning is linked to empowerment (control over outcomes). Argues LLM causal-looking output reflects text written by human causal modellers.
numbers: Intro cites Jin et al. 2024, Lewis and Mitchell 2024, Kosoy et al. 2022 as showing limited LLM causal inference. Human effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Argument partly interpretive; I did not read the human results section closely.
agent_relevance: Idea: prefer tests whose outcome the agent can control or vary, a computable proxy for a good intervention.

source: Gopnik et al. (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history (as cited by Samiei et al. 2026)
finding: As reported by Samiei et al.: adults infer conjunctive rules worse than children from passive ambiguous data; rule-inference accuracy is plotted from 4-year-olds to adults.
numbers: Figure values not mapped to groups in the extracted text, so none assigned.
limits: Second-hand; open the PNAS paper for exact numbers.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the children-as-flat-prior claim in GX-Chen 2025.

source: Schulz, Gopnik, Glymour (2007) and Sobel and Kushnir (2006), as cited by Samiei et al. (2026)
finding: As reported by Samiei et al.: learners learn more when they choose their own interventions than when told what to do; preschoolers learn causal structure from conditional interventions.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand citation only.
agent_relevance: Supports letting the agent choose its test inside code-checked limits rather than following a fixed script.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: More reasoning effort did not remove the disjunctive bias in general. Hypothesis-elimination efficiency was measured for the o-mini series at several reasoning-effort levels.
numbers: Fig. 12: GPT o-mini reasoning-effort sweep. deepseek-reasoner was the one model near-perfect with oracle data.
limits: Exact numbers in figures, not copied.
agent_relevance: More test-time thinking is not the fix; changing the hypothesis set is.
